questions.problem: Given $X∼B(7,0.6),$ compute $P(1<X\le 3).$ Round your final answer to $4$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(7,0.6),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.6)^{x}(0.4)^{7-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1<X\le 3) & =P(X\in \{2,3\}) \\  & =f(2)+f(3) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})(0.6)^{2}(0.4)^{7-2}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{3})(0.6)^{3}(0.4)^{7-3} \\  & =21(0.6)^{2}(0.4)^{5}+35(0.6)^{3}(0.4)^{4} \\  & ≈0.2710\end{aligned}
$$

to $4$ decimal places.

questions.problem: Given that $X∼B(9,0.3),$ compute $P(X\le 7).$ Round your final answer to $4$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(9,0.3),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{9}{x})(0.3)^{x}(0.7)^{9-x}.
$$

Computing $P(X\le 7)$ will require us to compute $f(x)$ at $x=0,1,2,…,7.$ However, if we compute the complement $P(X>7)$ instead, then we will only have to compute $f(x)$ at $x=8,9,$ which will result in a much faster computation.

Computing $P(X>7),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X>7) & =P(X\in \{8,9\}) \\  & =f(8)+f(9) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{9}{8})(0.3)^{8}(0.7)^{9-8}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{9}{9})(0.3)^{9}(0.7)^{9-9} \\  & =9(0.3)^{8}(0.7)+(0.3)^{9} \\  & ≈0.0004\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 7) & =1-P(X>7) \\  & ≈1-0.0004 \\  & =0.9996\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

questions.problem: Given that $X∼B(7,0.4),$ compute $P(X\le 2).$ Round your final answer to $4$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial,  we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(7,0.4),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{x})(0.4)^{x}(0.6)^{7-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\le 2) & =P(X\in \{0,1,2\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1)+f(2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{0})(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{7-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{1})(0.4)^{1}(0.6)^{7-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{7}{2})(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{7-2} \\  & =1(0.4)^{0}(0.6)^{7}+7(0.4)(0.6)^{6}+21(0.4)^{2}(0.6)^{5} \\  & ≈0.4199\end{aligned}
$$

to $4$ decimal places.

questions.problem: Given that $X∼B(6,0.6),$ compute $P(X\ge 2).$ Round your final answer to $4$ decimal places.
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(6,0.6),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{x})(0.6)^{x}(0.4)^{6-x}.
$$

Computing $P(X\ge 2)$ will require us to compute $f(x)$ at $x=2,3,4,5,6.$ However, if we compute the complement $P(X<2)$ instead, then we will only have to compute $f(x)$ at $x=0,1,$ which will result in a much faster computation.

Computing $P(X<2),$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X<2) & =P(X\in \{0,1\}) \\  & =f(0)+f(1) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{0})(0.6)^{0}(0.4)^{6-0}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{6}{1})(0.6)^{1}(0.4)^{6-1} \\  & =1(0.6)^{0}(0.4)^{6}+6(0.6)^{1}(0.4)^{5} \\  & ≈0.0410\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(X\ge 2) & =1-P(X<2) \\  & ≈1-0.0410 \\  & =0.9590\end{aligned}
$$

rounded to $4$ decimal places.

questions.problem: If $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{3}),$  then, **rounded to $3$ decimal places**, $P(1\le X<3)≈${{field-1}} .
questions.worked_solution:
For a binomial random variable $X∼B(n,p),$ where $n$ is the number of trials, and $p$ is the probability of success on each trial, we have the following probability mass function:

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{n}{x}){p}^{x}(1-p)^{n-x}
$$

Here, we have $X∼B(4,\frac{1}{3}),$ so $X$ has the probability mass function

$$
f(x)=(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{x}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{x}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-x}.
$$

Therefore, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}P(1\le X<3) & =P(X\in \{1,2\}) \\  & =f(1)+f(2) \\  & =(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{1}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-1}+(\genfrac{}{}{0pt}{}{4}{2}){(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{4-2} \\  & =4{(\frac{1}{3})}^{1}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{3}+6{(\frac{1}{3})}^{2}{(\frac{2}{3})}^{2} \\  & ≈0.691\end{aligned}
$$

 
rounded to $3$ decimal places.
